Half of this wiki is written by people. The other half — [areas](/reference),
[declarations](/reference/symbols), [GSC builtins](/reference/gsc) and [source
files](/reference/files) — is generated by reading every C, C++ and assembly
file in the tree.

Knowing exactly what that generator does is the difference between trusting it
correctly and trusting it too much.

## What it is

A **lexical scan**. It reads the checked-in text, blanks comments and
preprocessor directives while preserving every byte offset, and matches
declaration shapes. From that it records structs, unions, enums, classes,
typedefs, function definitions, prototypes, macros and assembly labels, each
with its file, line and the doc comment immediately above it.

It also finds every `Scr_AddFunction` / `Scr_AddMethod` call and resolves the
bound symbol to its definition, which is what produces the builtin list.

## What it is not

- **It does not preprocess.** A declaration produced by a macro is invisible to
  it. A declaration inside a disabled `#ifdef` is still listed.
- **It does not link.** "Defined in" means a definition with that name was found
  in the text, not that the linker chose it. Two static functions with the same
  name in different translation units both appear.
- **It does not compute layout.** Struct members are listed in declaration
  order with no byte offsets, because this tree uses packing pragmas and layout
  is a compiler question. See [the packing hazard](/wiki/source-layout).
- **It does not check behaviour.** That a function exists, is declared and has a
  doc comment says nothing about whether it is correct against a real client.

Every entry carries its file and line so you can check the source. That is the
point of the design: the index is an index, not an authority.

## The implementation badge

Every callable is labelled with how it is actually implemented.

| Badge | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **C** / **C++** | A definition in this repository, in that language. |
| **x86 asm** | The only definition found is an assembly label in `src/asmsource/`. This is retained disassembly from the original game binary, not a rewrite. See [Retained x86 assembly](/wiki/retained-assembly). |
| **no definition found** | Declared, but no definition was found anywhere. A prompt to look, not a verdict: macro-generated, vendored, or genuinely missing. |

From the last index run: **12,651 C**, **1,812 C++**, **3,512 x86 asm** and
**1,529 unresolved**. Roughly one in five callables in this server is retained
assembly.

## Areas

An area is a directory family, and it is resolved from the file a declaration
lives in, not from where it is used. That is why a GSC builtin registered in
`src/scr_vm_main.c` is filed under the area of the function it binds to — the
registration site is the same file for nearly everything, so it would tell you
nothing.

The nine CoDOL areas are marked as such; `engine`, `asmsource`, `platform`,
`vendor`, `tools` and `tests` are not.

`tools/cod4_dasm/` — the full ~1.8 million-line CoD4 disassembly that
`src/asmsource/` was drawn from — is deliberately **not** indexed. It is not
server source and it would swamp everything else.

## Searching

The search box covers all three kinds of content at once. Prose is matched with
Postgres full-text search, so quoted phrases and `-excluded` words work.
Identifiers are additionally matched by **prefix**, because no stemmer would
relate `CODOL_Write` to `CODOL_WriteSnapshotDeltaNumber`.

Authored pages rank above generated entries for the same query, on the
assumption that if somebody wrote a page about a thing, that page is the better
starting point.

## Keeping it current

The index is a snapshot. Rebuild it after changing the source:

```sh
cd wiki/backend
python -m app.cli index
```

Each run is recorded with the git commit it read, and the front page shows when
the last one finished. Every source file is listed with its sha256, so a claim
made on a wiki page can be checked against the file it was written from.

Rebuilding replaces the reference tables wholesale. It never touches authored
pages, their revisions, or accounts.
